title: What does it take to sustain job creation? Lessons from five countries
gist: Analyzing five historical episodes of sustained employment growth (Australia, Chile, Colombia, Korea, Singapore), World Bank economists find no single formula but a repeatable three-pillar policy framework -- infrastructure, business-environment reform, and private capital mobilization -- for EMDEs facing a record 1.2 billion-person youth employment wave by 2035.

insights.claim: Between 2025 and 2035, roughly 1.2 billion young people in emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) will reach working age, the largest youth cohort the world has likely ever seen.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Signals a decade-defining scale of labor-market absorption needed in developing economies, relevant to sizing consumer and labor markets and social-stability risk.
insights.quote: around 1.2 billion young people in these economies are expected to reach working age, the largest youth cohort the world will likely ever see, according to a new World Bank Group study.

insights.claim: Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East and North Africa will see the largest inflows of young people into working age that these regions have ever recorded.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: These regions face the sharpest near-term pressure to create jobs at scale, raising political and investment risk if job creation lags.
insights.quote: In Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East and North Africa, the coming wave of young people will be the largest these regions have seen to date.

themes.theme: Five historical episodes of sustained job growth

insights.claim: Australia (1994-2008), Chile (1979-92), Colombia (2002-08), South Korea (1986-97), and Singapore (2004-14) each sustained strong employment growth for prolonged periods, identified by an algorithm requiring a rising employment-to-population ratio for at least seven years.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Gives policymakers and investors a benchmark set of real-world case studies for what durable job-creation booms look like and how long they can last.
insights.quote: Australia (1994-2008), Chile (1979-92), Colombia (2002-08), the Republic of Korea (1986-97), and Singapore (2004-14) all experienced prolonged periods of strong employment growth
insights.locator: Five episodes of sustained job creation

insights.claim: During these five sustained job-creation episodes, employment grew by an average of 3.4 percent a year, roughly twice the pace seen in other years, alongside rising labor force participation and falling unemployment.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Quantifies how much faster labor markets can expand under the right conditions, a yardstick for evaluating current EMDE reform programs.
insights.quote: employment grew by an average of 3.4 percent a year, roughly twice the pace recorded in other years

insights.claim: Investment growth averaged nearly 10 percent a year during the five job-creation episodes, almost four times the rate seen outside those periods.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Points to investment mobilization, not just labor policy, as the core engine behind durable job booms.
insights.quote: investment growth averaged nearly 10 percent a year, almost four times higher than in other years

insights.claim: Output growth was roughly 50 percent higher during the five sustained job-creation episodes than in years outside them, alongside solid productivity growth.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Confirms sustained job-creation episodes coincide with broad-based macroeconomic outperformance, not just labor-market statistics.
insights.quote: output growth was roughly 50 percent higher than outside these episodes, and productivity growth was solid

insights.claim: In Chile and Colombia, natural resource development was enabled by robust infrastructure networks, while Singapore's rise as a regional logistics and financial hub rested on sustained investment in transport, digital connectivity, education, and public services.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Shows infrastructure investment as a precondition for both resource-led and services-led job-growth models.
insights.quote: Singapore's emergence as a regional logistics and financial hub rested on investment in transportation, digital connectivity, education, and public services.

insights.claim: Korea and Singapore moved up the value chain through innovation and workforce skills, with rising educational attainment helping align workers' skills with evolving firm demand.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Highlights skills upgrading as a mechanism connecting education policy to sustained employment growth in higher-value industries.
insights.quote: Korea and Singapore moved up the value chain through innovation and workforce skills

insights.claim: Chile's fiscal reforms and stronger central bank autonomy improved macroeconomic credibility and price stability, supporting its sustained job-creation episode.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Illustrates how monetary and fiscal credibility reforms can be a direct lever for job creation, not just inflation control.
insights.quote: In Chile, fiscal reforms and stronger central bank autonomy helped improve macroeconomic credibility and price stability.

insights.claim: Colombia adopted inflation targeting, improved tax administration, introduced debt sustainability guidelines, and implemented labor market reforms, which together reduced informality and underemployment and accelerated job creation, especially among young people.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Provides a concrete reform bundle other EMDEs could benchmark when designing youth employment strategies.
insights.quote: Colombia adopted inflation targeting, improved tax administration, induced debt sustainability guidelines, and implemented labor market reforms.

insights.claim: Chile's pension reform deepened domestic capital markets, Korea's National Pension Scheme channeled assets into public infrastructure, Singapore expanded public-private partnerships, and Colombia privatized banks and strengthened corporate governance -- all as vehicles for mobilizing private capital toward job-creating investment.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Maps specific financial-sector reform channels (pensions, PPPs, privatization) that translated into real-economy job creation.
insights.quote: Chile's pension reform deepened domestic capital markets; Korea's National Pension Scheme channeled assets into public infrastructure and capital markets; Singapore expanded public-private partnerships; and Colombia privatized banks and strengthened corporate governance.

themes.theme: No silver bullet, but a repeatable framework

insights.claim: There is no single formula for sustained job creation, but the five country experiences show a consistent framework of complementary, mutually reinforcing policies across infrastructure, business environment, and capital mobilization.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Argues policymakers should pursue coordinated multi-pillar reform packages rather than isolated interventions when targeting job creation.
insights.quote: There is no “silver bullet” solution for durably generating jobs at scale.
